content.p: On the last Wednesday of the 1927 school year, the north wing of Bath Consolidated School in Bath Township, Michigan, was blown apart while its pupils sat at their desks. About half an hour later a second blast, set off in front of the ruins as neighbours dug for survivors, killed the man who had caused both. He was Andrew Kehoe, a farmer and the school board's own treasurer. Most modern accounts count 45 dead including Kehoe, 38 of them children. It remains the deadliest attack on a school in United States history.
A coroner's jury sitting in the village within days found that the explosions were the result of a premeditated plan and that Kehoe had carried it out alone.
content.h2: A school that cost more than the farm could bear
content.p: Bath was a farming village of about 300 people. In 1922 it opened a consolidated school that replaced a scatter of one-room country schools and took pupils from kindergarten through high school; the 1926 census counted 314 scholars. According to 9and10News, local taxes on each thousand dollars of valuation rose from $12.26 in 1922 to $19.80 by 1926, and the school's costs were a standing grievance for Kehoe.

Kehoe was born on 1 February 1872 near Tecumseh, Michigan, one of 13 children, and trained in electrical engineering at Michigan State College. He bought a farm near Bath and moved there in 1919. Accounts of him agree that he was frugal, hot-tempered and difficult. A&E says he was suspected of needlessly killing animals, among them a neighbour's dog and one of his own horses; 9and10News, quoting a neighbour's account, says he admitted shooting the dog. Locals called him the "dynamite farmer", the New York Times reported in 1927, because he was forever blasting stumps and rocks.

Voters put him on the school board in 1924, hoping, A&E says, that his stinginess would discipline the budget. On the board he was obstructive and often clashed with Superintendent Emory Huyck. 9and10News says he tried more than once to have the man dismissed. In 1925 he was appointed township clerk for the remainder of a term, but he lost the election for the post the following spring. ClickOnDetroit says he then faced foreclosure on his farm, having stopped paying the mortgage, and that his wife Nellie was ill with tuberculosis. A&E gives her condition as either asthma or tuberculosis.

Historians and journalists describe these pressures as a trigger rather than a proven cause. Harold Schechter, who has written a book on the case, told WKAR that by spring 1927 Kehoe had become paranoid and believed the townspeople had ruined him financially by voting for the expensive school.
content.h2: Months of preparation in plain sight
content.p: Kehoe's position gave him the run of the building. Over the summer of 1926 he did repair work at the school, which gave him long, unsupervised access, 9and10News reports, and A&E says he managed many maintenance tasks there, working on its plumbing, heating and electrical systems. ClickOnDetroit says he bought two boxes of dynamite in Lansing in the autumn of 1926, which raised no alarm because farmers commonly used it. The 10 Minute Murder podcast adds that locals heard blasts from his farm through the summer of 1926, and that he explained them as stump clearing.

Evidence given at the inquest, reported by the St. Johns Republican-News on 26 May 1927, shows how little anyone suspected. Joseph T. Sleight, a neighbour, said the community had been shaken by a blast the previous New Year's Eve, caused by explosives on Kehoe's farm that were fired with an electrically controlled alarm clock. Sleight told the prosecutor he had no reason to think Kehoe had an accomplice. The paper said the hidden charge was several hundred pounds of pyrotol and dynamite spread beneath the school floor and linked by wire to two batteries and to a timing clock in the sub-basement.

Some neighbours recalled strange remarks afterwards. ClickOnDetroit reports testimony from Sidney Howell that Kehoe told him and three boys, after the fire at the farm began, "You better get out of here, you better go down to the school." Kindergarten teacher Bernice Sterling said that when she asked to use Kehoe's woods for a picnic he told her, "If you are going to have a picnic, you would best have it right away." David Harte, who lived across the road, said he thought the plot had been in the works for months.

The last board meeting Kehoe attended was on 5 May 1927, 13 days before the attack, 9and10News says. According to the Republican-News, the school's janitor Frank Smith testified that Kehoe's last words to him in the basement shortly before the explosion were "I'm in an awful hurry".

Accounts disagree on the time. The Republican-News, reporting the inquest the following week, said the clock was set for about 9:45 a.m. and ClickOnDetroit and 10 Minute Murder also give 9:45. A&E and Slate say 8:45. The sources agree on what followed. The blast brought down the roof and upper storey of the north wing. Teacher Bernice Sterling told the Associated Press that she saw the bodies of her children hurled against the walls and through windows. A surviving teacher quoted by 10 Minute Murder remembered children tossed high in the air and some thrown out of the building.

George Robson, whose parents were pupils that morning, told 9and10News his mother's account. Her teacher that day was Superintendent Huyck, who told students not to panic or try to jump from the second-floor windows, and men working in town that week for what is now Consumers Energy arrived with ladders. Byron Robson, the senior class president, had just waved to her through the hallway glass on his way to the church next door, where graduation was to be held. Both survived. A&E notes that rescuers who had seen the First World War were sickened by what they found.

At the farm, about a mile down the road, the house and barn were burning. Nellie Kehoe was dead. Her body was found the next day: ClickOnDetroit says her skull was crushed, A&E says she had several broken bones, and Arnie Bernstein's description of his book says her remains were tied to a hand cart. The Republican-News said the inquest concluded that Kehoe killed his wife at some time between Monday night and Wednesday morning, and burned her body along with his buildings on Wednesday. A&E and 9and10News say Kehoe's two horses were tied in the barn with their feet wired together. Investigators later found a sign wired to a fence on the property. It read: "Criminals are made, not born."

About 30 minutes after the first blast, ClickOnDetroit and Slate say, Kehoe drove up to the school in a vehicle packed with dynamite and with scrap metal and tools to act as shrapnel. 9and10News describes the car as a Model T. Huyck was helping with the wounded when Kehoe called him over. Kehoe set off the load, killing himself, Huyck and others close by.

The number of others killed varies. ClickOnDetroit and 9and10News say four besides Kehoe, including the superintendent; A&E says several children and rescuers died with them. According to the Republican-News, the village postmaster, Glenn Smith, was fatally injured in the explosion and died before reaching hospital. 9and10News says the blast also sent a piece of steel through the picture window of a house three blocks away, close to where a surviving student had just crossed the road.

When rescuers went through the wreckage they found a great deal more explosive. The Republican-News said 504 pounds of pyrotol and dynamite had failed to go off because the batteries were not strong enough, while ClickOnDetroit and Slate refer to a short circuit and to more than 500 pounds under the south wing. ClickOnDetroit adds that police also found a gasoline container rigged to ignite a spark, which investigators believed was a backup. Had everything exploded, Schechter told WKAR, Kehoe would have killed "an entire generation of children in that community". A&E likewise says the entire school would have been destroyed had the south-wing charge fired.

There is no single agreed figure. A&E, Slate, ClickOnDetroit and 10 Minute Murder count 45 dead, Kehoe among them, with 38 children. WKAR and Bernstein write of 38 children and six adults killed. A&E breaks its total into 38 children and seven adults including Kehoe. NPR's 2009 StoryCorps piece said 39 people were killed. 9and10News described 38 students and three adults killed in the school blast with 50 injured, against 58 hurt in A&E and ClickOnDetroit.

The inquest's own wording differs again. The Republican-News reported that the coroner's jury held that 37 school children and 7 adults died as a result of Kehoe's plan. Michigan Radio reports a later death that bears on the count: that Richard Fritz, whose sister Marjorie also died, died in 1928 of injuries from the bombing and went without a gravestone until 2014, when a man writing a book about the 1927 bombing paid for one.

Survivors carried the injuries for life. Donald Huffman, who was nine, told StoryCorps that he lost an eye and part of his cheekbone, and that three children from one family were killed outright. Johanna Cushman-Balzer, whose mother Wilma was at the school, told NPR, as A&E quotes her, that as a child she learned not to ask about scars, because the answer was always the Bath school disaster.

A preliminary inquiry was ordered by state fire marshal Charles Lane. Prosecutor William C. Searl questioned a dozen witnesses, and the Republican-News said the main fact it established was that Kehoe had no accomplice. Lane himself had doubted that one man could have done the wiring, ClickOnDetroit says, and thought the volume of explosive too great to have been carried in small amounts night after night.

The formal inquest opened on Monday at the Bath community hall before Coroner C. E. Lamb, with Searl questioning some 40 witnesses over three days, the St. Johns paper said. It named six jurors, among them Edward Drumheller and Clarence Tolman. ClickOnDetroit gives a longer period of testimony, saying it ran for a week.

The jury's verdict, printed by the paper, was that Kehoe "was sane at all times" and "so concealed his operations that there was no cause to suspicion any of his actions". It also found that the school board and janitor Frank Smith were not negligent and not guilty of negligence in failing to discover the plan. Slate says the inquest determined that Kehoe acted alone. ClickOnDetroit says the school board was cleared.
Kehoe's body was claimed by his sister and buried in an unmarked grave in Clinton County, ClickOnDetroit reports.

Donations arrived from across the country. Monty Ellsworth, a neighbour quoted by Slate, remembered thousands of cars stopping on the Lansing road, a double row of traffic all day, without a single horn. On 23 June 1927 the Republican-News itemised the first group of relief money received: $748.15 through the Red Cross, $2,500 from the Clinton County supervisors and $2,000 from the Governor's committee. It also said that Senator James Couzens, with Governor Green, had spent the previous Thursday in Bath and visited injured children in Lansing hospitals.

School resumed on 5 September 1927 in the community hall, ClickOnDetroit says. Couzens gave $75,000 towards a new building on 15 September, the Lansing architect Warren Holmes donated plans, and the rebuilt school, with its new wing, was named the James Couzens Agricultural School.

The national attention was short. Three days after the explosion Charles Lindbergh landed in Paris, which Schechter and Bernstein both say pushed Bath out of the papers. Many survivors rarely spoke of it. One told Local 4 that they never swapped memories, and wondered whether counselling would have helped. George Robson said his parents made a deliberate effort to move on and never talked about the day.

The building was demolished in 1975 and the site became a memorial park, ClickOnDetroit says; the cupola that crowned the school survived the blasts and is a feature of the park, according to A&E. A Michigan Historical Marker with the victims' names was installed in 1991.
